procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 23.02.2018 of the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in I. A. No. 892 of 2018 in Crl. Appeal (SJ) No. 176 of 2018.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted and sentenced by the Trial Court under sections 420, 467, 468, 471 r/w 120-B IPC. The appellant filed Criminal Appeal No. 176 of 2018 before the High Court challenging the conviction and sentence. The appellant also filed an application for suspension of sentence. The High Court allowed the application for suspension of sentence and granted bail, but directed the appellant to deposit the fine amount awarded by the Trial Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant challenged the High Court's direction to deposit the fine amount before the Supreme Court, arguing that the fine should have been automatically stayed under s.357(2) Cr.P.C. The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's direction, holding that s.357(2) Cr.P.C. was not applicable in this case because there was no order of payment of compensation out of the fine imposed by the trial court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the imposition of a fine, as part of a sentence, is automatically stayed under Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. pending the decision of an appeal.

facts: The appellant was convicted by a Trial Court and sentenced to imprisonment along with a fine.
The appellant filed an appeal in the High Court and an application to suspend the sentence.
The High Court suspended the prison sentence but, as a condition, directed the appellant to deposit the fine amount.
The appellant challenged this direction, arguing that under Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C., the fine was automatically stayed because an appeal had been filed.
Crucially, the Trial Court had not issued any order to pay compensation to a victim out of the fine amount collected.
law: The Court interpreted Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. by reading it in conjunction with Section 357(1).
Section 357(1) allows a court to order that a fine be used to pay compensation to a victim.
Section 357(2) states that "no such payment" of compensation shall be made to the victim until the time for appeal has passed or, if an appeal is filed, until the appeal is decided.
The purpose of this provision is to prevent a situation where compensation is paid out and then becomes difficult to recover if the conviction is later overturned on appeal.
The Court clarified that Section 357(2) only creates an embargo on the *utilization* of the fine for paying compensation; it does not stay the sentence of the fine itself.
The power to suspend a sentence, including a fine, is governed by a different provision, Section 389 of the Cr.P.C., which gives the appellate court discretion to impose conditions.
application: The Court determined that Section 357(2) was not applicable in this specific case.
This was because the Trial Court had not made any order under Section 357(1) to use the fine to pay compensation to a victim.
Since there was no order for payment of compensation, the provision in Section 357(2) that stays "such payment" was not triggered.

The High Court's direction to deposit the fine was not a violation of Section 357(2) but rather a valid exercise of its discretionary power under Section 389 of the Cr.P.C. while granting the suspension of the sentence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument and held that the imposition of a fine is not automatically stayed under Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. when an appeal is filed. This section only stays the payment of compensation out of the fine to a victim, and only applies when a specific order for such compensation has been made. Therefore, the High Court was correct in directing the appellant to deposit the fine amount as a condition for suspending the sentence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the imposition of a fine, as part of a sentence, is automatically stayed under Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. pending the decision of an appeal.
appellant_arguments: A plain, literal interpretation of Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. indicates that the payment of a fine is automatically suspended when an appeal is filed.
The precedent case of Stanny Felix Pinto v. Jangid Builders Pvt. Ltd. is not applicable because the court in that case did not consider or interpret Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C.
The judgment in K.C. Sareen vs. C.B.I. Chandigarh supports the appellant's position.
The trial judge's direction to pay was unreasonable, especially since the appellant's liability was vicarious under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.
respondent_arguments: The appellate court has the authority to direct an accused to deposit the fine amount pending appeal, as upheld in the case of Stanny Felix Pinto v. Jangid Builders Pvt. Ltd.
Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. does not provide an absolute, automatic stay that would prevent an appellate court from imposing a condition to deposit the fine.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A literal interpretation and plain reading of sub-section (2) of Section 357 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be accepted.
obiter: A section heading or marginal note can be relied upon to clear any doubt or ambiguity in the interpretation of a provision and to discern the legislative intent.
No unreasonable amount of compensation can be directed to be paid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that Section 357(2) of the Cr.P.C. does not provide for an automatic stay on the deposit of a fine imposed by a trial court pending an appeal. The court interpreted the provision to mean that what is stayed is the 'application of fine' (i.e., its payment to a victim), not the appellate court's power to impose a condition for its deposit as part of an order suspending the sentence.
legal_tests_applied: Statutory Interpretation: The court sought to determine the 'intention of the lawmaker and the object sought to be achieved' by analyzing the language of Section 357.
Reasonableness of Compensation: The court applied a test that 'the amount of compensation must be a reasonable sum' and that 'no unreasonable amount of compensation can be directed to be paid.'
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the appellant's literal interpretation of Section 357(2), stating: 'Sub-section (2) of Section 357 uses the word “fine”. It does not say that what would be stayed i.e. application of fine. Sub-section (2) of Section 357, in our opinion, does not contemplate any other interpretation.'

The precedents relied upon by the appellant were found to be unhelpful, with the court concluding: 'neither Section 357(2) of the Cr. P.C. nor the decision relied on for the petitioners is of any help to the petitioners.'

The court provided an alternative basis for its decision, noting that even if the appellant's argument on Section 357(2) were accepted, Section 357(3) concerning compensation would still be applicable: 'Even assuming that Mr Lalit was correct in his submission, still then sub-section (3) would be squarely attracted.'
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the underlying principle of the respondent's argument that an appellate court has the power to impose a condition for depositing the fine amount, as upheld in cases like Stanny Felix Pinto, even while acknowledging that the specific statutory provision of Section 357(2) was not considered in that precedent.

The court's own interpretation of Section 357(2) aligned with the respondent's position that the stay is not absolute and does not prevent an appellate court from ordering a deposit of the fine pending appeal.
policy_considerations: The court expressed a concern for fairness and proportionality in sentencing, stating that 'the amount of compensation must be a reasonable sum' and 'no unreasonable amount of compensation can be directed to be paid.'
